strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important gap: existing feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction models (DUSt3R, VGGT, π3) are restricted to pinhole/rectified imagery, while Wid3R is presented as the first feed-forward multi-view model supporting fisheye and 360° cameras.

The core technical recipe -- combining a ray-based spherical-harmonics representation (building on UniK3D) with a permutation-equivariant local-frame architecture (building on π3) and a novel trainable 'camera model token' for explicit camera-type conditioning -- is a sensible and reasonably well-motivated engineering synthesis for this problem.

Broad and diverse training corpus spanning pinhole, fisheye, and 360° datasets (TartanAirV2, ASE, Hypersim, KITTI-360, 360Loc, Matterport3D, ScanNet++, EDEN, VKITTI), along with tailored augmentation strategies (pinhole-to-fisheye reprojection, ERP rotation augmentation) that are appropriate for the wide-FoV setting.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple tasks (camera pose estimation, point-map estimation, large-scale visual localization, monocular 360° depth) and multiple real/synthetic benchmarks (FIORD, Zip-NeRF, Stanford2D3D, Matterport3D, ScanNet++), with consistent and often large improvements over VGGT and π3 baselines.

Practical efficiency advantage demonstrated in the large-scale localization experiment (feed-forward inference in ~3s vs ~30min for SfM-based IM360 pipeline), which is a meaningful applied contribution.
Reasonably thorough ablation study isolating the effects of camera-token conditioning, training-data camera-type composition, and batch frame count, providing some insight into design choices.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the ray/SH representation is adopted directly from UniK3D and the permutation-equivariant local-frame architecture from π3; the main new element is the camera model token, whose architectural details (how it is constructed, injected into the network, or whether it generalizes beyond three discrete camera categories) are described only briefly and lack sufficient technical depth for reproducibility.

The most natural and important baseline -- applying existing calibration/undistortion followed by VGGT or π3, which the paper explicitly motivates against in the introduction -- is never empirically compared; only the pinhole-only models applied directly to distorted images are used as baselines, which are guaranteed to fail and thus somewhat inflate the apparent improvement.

In the monocular 360° depth comparison (Table 6), Wid3R's Abs Rel (0.227) is substantially worse than several specialized single-view 360° methods (e.g., Elite360D 0.105, Depth Anywhere 0.085), which weakens the claim of 'comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art methods'; the paper does not adequately reconcile or discuss this discrepancy.

360° training data constitutes <1% of the total training set, raising concerns about how well the reported 360° results generalize beyond the specific curated benchmarks (Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D) used for evaluation.

No analysis of model size, parameter/compute overhead introduced by the camera token and dual angular/radial heads relative to the π3 backbone, nor detailed inference-time comparison against VGGT/π3 on comparable hardware/settings (only the localization pipeline timing is given).

Dynamic scenes are explicitly excluded, which is a reasonable scope limitation but somewhat narrows the claimed generality of 'wide field-of-view 3D reconstruction' for real-world robotics/AR-VR applications mentioned in the introduction.

Some presentation issues (e.g., ambiguous notation such as radial distance used as a weight that could be zero/small causing instability in Eq. 2-3, and limited explanation of how the camera-model token is selected/assigned at test time for camera types not seen during training) reduce clarity and reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a clear and practically important gap: existing feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction methods (DUSt3R, VGGT, π3) are restricted to pinhole/rectified imagery, while Wid3R is presented as the first feed-forward multi-view model to directly handle fisheye and full 360° (equirectangular) imagery without calibration/undistortion preprocessing.

The technical approach is coherent: it combines a spherical-harmonics ray/pencil-of-rays representation (extending UniK3D's monocular formulation to the multi-view, permutation-equivariant setting of π3) with a lightweight, trainable camera-model token that explicitly conditions the angular module on camera type, offering an interpretable mechanism for distortion-aware prediction.

Experimental coverage is broad and convincing for the claimed scope: zero-shot camera pose estimation (FIORD, Zip-NeRF, Stanford2D3D), large-scale localization on Matterport3D, dense point-map estimation on three datasets, and monocular 360° depth on Matterport3D against many specialized single-view 360° baselines, with consistent and often large improvements over VGGT/π3.

The ablation study (Table 7) is informative, isolating the effects of the camera-model token, cross-camera-model training data composition, and batch frame count, and providing a plausible explanation (reduced overfitting from data diversity) for why mixing camera types improves 360° performance despite limited native 360° supervision (<1% of training data).

The training-data curation, augmentation strategy (pinhole→fisheye reprojection with softmax splatting; ERP rotation augmentation), and overlap-aware sampling strategy are described with enough detail to be largely reproducible and are sensible engineering choices for the sparse-view, wide-baseline regime typical of wide-FoV capture.
weaknesses: The core novelty is primarily an integration of existing components (UniK3D's spherical-harmonics ray formulation, π3's permutation-equivariant local-frame architecture, and a calibration-token idea similar to prior monocular adaptation work [19]) rather than a fundamentally new representation or architecture; the paper would benefit from more explicitly delineating what is technically new versus adapted, and the camera-model token's exact integration mechanism (concatenation vs. cross-attention, dimensionality, how it interacts with the angular module) is under-specified.

Comparisons against wide-FoV-specific baselines beyond VGGT/π3 are limited for pose and point-map tasks; the more relevant SfM/localization competitor IM360 (Table 4) is not uniformly outperformed (e.g., lower Acc./AUC on one scene, 2t7WUuJeko7), which somewhat tempers the "consistently outperforms" framing used elsewhere in the paper.

For the fisheye benchmarks (FIORD, Zip-NeRF) no ground-truth point clouds appear to be available (marked N/A in Fig. 5), so point-map/geometric accuracy on fisheye imagery is not directly validated the way it is for 360° datasets, leaving pose-only zero-shot metrics as the main fisheye evidence.

The overall loss function has many hand-set weighting hyperparameters (λ_normal, λ_pose, λ_ray, λ_rad, λ_uncer) with no sensitivity analysis, and the paper does not report compute/training-time budget or model size comparisons to VGGT/π3, which would help assess practical trade-offs.

The acknowledged limitation regarding dynamic scenes is reasonable, but the paper offers no quantitative characterization of failure modes (e.g., under extreme distortion, very low overlap, or severe fisheye periphery) beyond qualitative figures, which would strengthen the honesty and completeness of the evaluation.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important gap: existing feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction methods (DUSt3R, VGGT, pi^3) assume pinhole/rectified imagery, while this paper is (to the authors' knowledge) the first multi-frame feed-forward network that operates directly on distorted wide-FoV imagery (fisheye and 360-degree) without calibration/undistortion.

The technical design is coherent and well-motivated: decoupling the point-map head into an angular module (spherical-harmonics-based ray prediction) and a radial module, plus a learned camera-model token for explicit conditioning, is a sensible way to inject camera-type awareness into an otherwise generic permutation-equivariant architecture (built on pi^3/UniK3D).

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive, spanning camera pose estimation (FIORD, Zip-NeRF, Stanford2D3D), point-map estimation (ScanNet++, Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D), large-scale localization (Matterport3D), and monocular 360 depth, showing consistent and often large improvements over VGGT and pi^3 baselines under distortion.

Useful ablation studies quantify the effect of camera-model token conditioning, training-data composition (imbalance of 360 data), and number of frames per batch, providing insight into why the approach helps particularly on data-scarce 360 imagery.

The supplementary material adds valuable context: a comparison against a cubemap-transformation baseline showing the practical drawbacks (efficiency, calibration dependence) of naive undistortion pipelines, and a forward-looking exploration of applying the method to panorama-based scene generation.

Reasonable reproducibility: loss formulations, training datasets, hyperparameters, and data augmentation strategies (fisheye reprojection, ERP rotation augmentation) are described in enough detail to support replication.
weaknesses: The camera model token requires the network to select among a small number of discrete pre-defined camera categories (pinhole/fisheye/360); it is unclear how the method generalizes to camera geometries or distortion profiles outside these three trained categories, or how the token is selected/inferred at test time for genuinely uncalibrated inputs — this partially undercuts the 'without explicit calibration' framing.

Training data for 360-degree cameras is extremely scarce (<1% of total), and while the ablation addresses this, the paper does not clearly discuss failure modes or remaining artifacts under more extreme distortion or unseen camera configurations beyond the tested benchmarks.

Comparisons are mostly against baselines not designed for wide-FoV inputs (VGGT, pi^3); more direct quantitative comparison against dedicated single/pairwise wide-FoV baselines (e.g., UniK3D itself, Dust3R with distortion handling) in the multi-view setting would strengthen the claims, since Table 1's qualitative comparison chart is not matched by full quantitative benchmarking against all listed related methods.

Some result tables (e.g., Table 4) are difficult to read/verify due to rendering/resolution issues, and statistical variance (e.g., across repeated samplings in Stanford2D3D/FIORD) is not reported, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported gains.

Runtime/efficiency analysis is limited to a single anecdotal claim (localization within three seconds); a more systematic comparison of inference cost/model size relative to VGGT/pi^3 and classical SfM pipelines would help substantiate claimed computational advantages.

The core contribution is largely an integration of existing components (UniK3D's SH-based ray representation, pi^3's permutation-equivariant multi-view backbone) with an added camera-token conditioning mechanism; while effective, the novelty is more architectural/integrative than conceptually new, which should temper claims of a fundamentally new capability.

strengths: Addresses a clear and practical gap: existing feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction methods (DUSt3R, VGGT, π³) assume pinhole/rectified images and fail to generalize to fisheye and 360° imagery; Wid3R is presented as the first multi-frame feed-forward network that directly handles distorted wide-FoV images without calibration/undistortion.

The technical design is reasonable and well-motivated: a ray-based representation with spherical-harmonics angular module plus a decoupled radial module avoids the limitations of point-map heads under strong distortion, and the camera model token gives an explicit, lightweight mechanism to condition the shared architecture on different projection types.

Extensive empirical validation across many datasets/tasks (pose estimation, point map estimation, large-scale localization, monocular 360° depth) and both synthetic and real data, with consistent and often large improvements over strong recent baselines (VGGT, π³) as well as specialized 360°/fisheye methods.

Useful ablations (Table 7) isolating the effect of camera-model-token conditioning, training data composition (pinhole/fisheye/sphere mixing), and batch size, showing that diverse-camera co-training benefits the underrepresented 360° regime — an insightful practical finding about data sparsity mitigation.

Reasonable practical/systems value: large-scale localization results show comparable accuracy to SfM-based pipelines (IM360+EDM) with drastically reduced runtime (seconds vs. minutes), which is a meaningful applied contribution beyond raw accuracy numbers.

Supplementary material provides useful additional context, including architecture ablations (self-attention vs cross-attention in the radial module), a demonstration that naive cubemap-based adaptation of pinhole-only models is inefficient/inferior, and exploratory application to panorama-based scene generation, indicating some awareness of broader applicability and limitations.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental/combinatorial: the architecture largely builds on π³ (permutation-equivariant backbone, pretrained weights) and UniK3D (ray/spherical-harmonics angular representation), with the main new elements being the camera-model token and self-attention-vs-cross-attention change in the radial module; the paper could more clearly delineate what is genuinely new versus adapted from these two prior works.

The 360° training data is stated to be <1% of total training data, and evaluation on 360° benchmarks (Stanford2D3D, Matterport3D) uses relatively small numbers of scenes/images (e.g., 2 scenes for Stanford2D3D, 18 scenes for Matterport3D); given the very large reported gains (e.g., +77.33 AUC on Stanford2D3D), the statistical robustness of these improvements (variance across seeds/splits, confidence intervals) is not reported.

Some qualitative baseline results (e.g., VGGT and π³ point clouds in Fig. 1 and Fig. 5) appear extremely degraded/collapsed on 360° data, raising the question of whether baselines were given a fair chance (e.g., appropriate preprocessing, cubemap conversion, or fine-tuning) — the supplementary does address one such comparison (cubemap→π³) but this is not systematically applied across all baseline comparisons in the main tables.

The paper does not report standard deviations, multiple training runs, or statistical significance for its main results tables, making it hard to judge how much of the reported improvement is robust versus dataset/sampling-dependent, especially given the random per-scene sampling procedures described (e.g., "repeating this sampling process 10 times per scene").

Limited discussion of failure cases or computational cost/training budget (parameter count, GPU-hours, inference latency per frame) relative to baselines beyond the single localization runtime comparison, which would help assess practicality and reproducibility.

Dynamic scenes are explicitly noted as unsupported (a fair, disclosed limitation), and the method still relies on a fixed maximum frame count constrained by GPU memory (limited to 12–24 frames), which may restrict scalability to very large-scale multi-hundred-image scenarios relative to sequential SfM pipelines.
